newsitem.title: FRANCE: Press says left win possible in French runoff poll.
newsitem.headline: Press says left win possible in French runoff poll.

text.p: French newspapers on Monday highlighted the sharp warning that voters have given the centre-right government, saying Sunday's first round of the parliamentary election meant the leftist bloc could win.
"Right flattened, left can win," the left-leaning Liberation said in a banner headline above a picture of a shortened Prime Minister Alain Juppe.

"Unprecedented repudiation of the parliamentary right," the daily Le Monde said. A cartoon showed President Jacques Chirac throwing a ballot box for Juppe, portrayed as a dog, to fetch. Chirac then frowns as Juppe returns with a far smaller box.

Voters gave the combined left a 4.5-point lead over the ruling centre-right coalition on Sunday and raised the prospect that Chirac may have to share power with a hostile, Socialist-led government after a runoff ballot on June 1.

Le Monde dubbed the election, called by Chirac in hopes of winning a like-minded majority to rule with him until 2002, a "boomerang poll". But it said the left was not sure of victory in a second round that was "open and unpredictable".

"The rebellion hits (Chirac), who had promoted this 'free hands for five years' operation, and his chief of staff Juppe, who already emerges as the first victim of this first round," Liberation's Serge July wrote in an editorial.
"The left has taken advantage of its governmental experience. It no longer scares people. European unification is not really threatened," July wrote.
The pro-government daily Le Figaro acknowledged the warning but was more cautious.
"What do the French want? They have delivered a sharp lesson to the right, which had been presented much too early as favourite," wrote Figaro editor Franz-Olivier Giesbert.
He said the outcome was still wide open.

"People have to be cautious about first-round results. They are often expressions of anger or friendship...Now the right can win only by changing its tone, its leaders and its message. It must offer a dream, a future, hopes," Giesbert said.

Alain Duhamel, political commentator for Europe 1 radio, said the left's lead corresponded to a mere one percentage point variation in the runoff vote. The high rate of abstentions -- 31.6 percent -- meant that the right had more reserves to draw on than the left.

"The French voted in the first round thinking that the right was the favourite. Now they wake up to see the left is favourite. They will think about their second-round vote in a different way," Duhamel said.

"Chirac will be under pressure to commit himself in the campaign even more. But naming a new prime minister would appear like capitulation to the enemy. He could however give two or three personalities a more prominent role, like (former premier) Edouard Balladur or (parliamentary speaker) Philippe Seguin," he added.
